parts.title: Earth Hour: Switching Off for the Planet
parts.directions: Read the passage and choose the best answer (A, B, C, or D) for each question.
passage: Imagine a city where, for one hour, the lights on famous buildings, bridges, and streets suddenly go out. This happens every year during Earth Hour, an event run by the World Wide Fund for Nature, which asks people to switch off unnecessary lights and think about the planet. Many people see it as a way to start a conversation about climate change. This passage explains how the idea began, what people do, and why some people disagree about its value.

Earth Hour began in Sydney, Australia, in 2007, when the environmental group WWF Australia worked with an advertising agency to plan a lights-off event. The first event took place on 31 March 2007, and its message was simple. Since then, the event has grown quickly and has reportedly reached about 190 countries and territories, including a digital version in 2020 because of COVID-19. The event is mainly **symbolic**, because its organisers say that the hour itself is meant to show concern rather than to save a large amount of energy.

Earth Hour usually takes place on the last Saturday of March, from 8.30 pm to 9.30 pm in each local time zone. Famous landmarks such as the Sydney Opera House, the Eiffel Tower, Big Ben, and the Empire State Building have joined in by going dark for the hour. Millions of ordinary people also switch off lights at home, and some spend the hour with family. Some people light candles, play board games, or tell stories, while others go for a walk and look at the stars. Some communities also hold small outdoor events that use very little electricity.

Not everyone agrees that Earth Hour is useful, and critics say that one hour without lights saves too little electricity to matter. A 2014 study of 274 measurements in ten countries reportedly found an average drop in electricity use of about four per cent, although results varied widely between cities. Some critics also argue that individual actions cannot replace decisions by governments and large companies. Supporters reply that the main goal is to raise awareness, and many organisers encourage people to make a **pledge** to change a daily habit, such as using less plastic or saving water.

Today, Earth Hour is about more than one hour in March, because WWF also supports projects such as planting forests and sharing wood-saving stoves in Madagascar. Some teachers use the day to talk about nature, and students often make posters about **their** favourite animals. Wherever you live, the idea is simple, and anyone can take part by turning off a few lights, learning something new, and sharing the message with friends. Whether or not the hour saves much energy, it reminds us that small actions, repeated by many people, can become a powerful message about caring for the planet.

parts.title: Daily Habits and the Architecture of a Healthy Life
parts.directions: Read the passage and choose the best answer (A, B, C, or D) for each question.
passage: Health is often imagined as the result of dramatic decisions, such as joining a gym or starting a diet, yet researchers suggest that most of it is built from small actions repeated every day. A 2002 study by Wood and colleagues reportedly found that about 43 per cent of daily behaviours are performed habitually, without much conscious thought. Seen this way, a healthy life is less a single achievement than an **incremental** structure built over time.

Psychologists describe a habit as a loop consisting of a cue, a routine, and a reward, and the craving for the reward is what keeps the loop turning. Because habits become linked to a context, such as a time of day, a place, or a previous action, they can feel almost automatic. A well-known 2009 study by Lally and colleagues found that automaticity took an average of 66 days. The range was wide, from 18 to 254 days, which suggests that the popular claim that habits form in twenty-one days is an oversimplification.

Physical activity is a clear example, because the World Health Organization (WHO) recommends at least 150 minutes of moderate-intensity activity per week for adults. Yet the organisation estimates that 31 per cent of adults, about 1.8 billion people, were insufficiently active in 2022, a rise of five percentage points since 2010. Among adolescents, roughly 80 per cent fall short of the recommended level.

Diet follows a similar pattern, and the WHO advises at least 400 grams of fruit and vegetables a day, under five grams of salt, and free sugars below ten per cent of energy. Few people can track such numbers precisely, so researchers often suggest simple rules, such as adding vegetables to every main meal. Small, repeatable rules are usually easier to follow than complicated plans that depend on willpower.

Environment matters as much as motivation, because people tend to repeat behaviours that are easy and visible. Keeping fruit on the kitchen table, laying out running shoes the night before, or linking a short walk to an existing routine, such as finishing a phone call, makes the healthy choice the default. Plans that demand dramatic change are rarely **sustainable**, whereas modest changes that fit into daily life are more likely to last.

Sleep and stress also shape health, and adults are commonly advised to aim for around seven to nine hours of sleep a night, although individual needs vary. Setbacks are normal, and habits can return when old cues reappear, which helps to explain why holidays and stressful weeks often disrupt routines. In these moments, the cues that trigger unhealthy habits are often stronger than **those** that support healthy ones, so planning for difficult situations is valuable. Research suggests that missing a single day rarely ruins a developing habit, so one lapse is not failure.

The architecture of a healthy life is therefore built from modest materials, namely regular movement, balanced meals, enough sleep, and routines that support them. No single habit guarantees health, and genetics, income, and environment also matter. Even so, small and consistent choices, repeated for weeks and months, give most people the best chance of building a life that remains healthy as they grow older.

parts.title: Technology in Education: Promise, Peril, and Pedagogy
parts.directions: Read the passage and choose the best answer (A, B, C, or D) for each question.
passage: Digital technology has become **pervasive** in education, from interactive whiteboards and learning platforms to tablets, online courses, and now artificial intelligence assistants. Its advocates promise personalised learning, wider access, and greater efficiency, while its critics warn of distraction, inequality, and a loss of human contact in the classroom. This passage weighs the promise against the peril and asks what good teaching requires.

UNESCO's 2023 Global Education Monitoring Report describes five channels through which technology affects education, including delivery, skills, and planning. At its best, adaptive software can give students immediate, personalised feedback and keep each learner working at a level that is challenging but achievable, while freeing teachers to spend time on discussion and support. Online courses and open resources can also reach people who live far from schools or universities.

The promise of access, however, depends on who is connected, and the pandemic made the gaps visible. As of April 2020, about 90 per cent of high-income countries reportedly offered online learning, compared with only about 25 per cent of low-income countries. Open online courses show a similar pattern, since only about three per cent of registrants reportedly come from low-income countries and just five to ten per cent complete a course. Technology can therefore widen existing inequalities when access, skills, and support are unevenly shared.

Evidence that devices improve learning is mixed, and a 2015 OECD study reportedly found that moderate computer users at school scored higher than rare users, while heavy users did worse. Phones and notifications are a particular worry, and UNESCO has described a shift from a handful of national initiatives to a widespread global trend of school phone bans. UNESCO also argues that technology reaches its potential only when access, regulation, and teacher preparation are in place.

Generative artificial intelligence has added a new layer of difficulty. **[1]** After ChatGPT was launched in November 2022, some school districts in the United States reportedly banned generative AI tools, although most of these bans were reversed within months. **[2]** Teachers worried that students might submit machine-written essays, and detection software was soon promoted as a solution. **[3]** For this reason, many educators now favour redesigning assignments, such as oral explanations and in-class drafts, over trying to police AI use. **[4]** Generative systems can also produce hallucinations, meaning confident but false statements, as well as biased answers, so the outputs need to be checked critically.

Teachers are central to any successful use of technology, and when teachers receive sustained training, **their** lessons may be more likely to use devices to deepen thinking rather than simply to entertain. Privacy is another concern, because learning platforms may collect large amounts of personal data about children, and parents and schools often have little information about how it is stored or used. Careful regulation and clear school policies can reduce these risks without banning useful tools.

The evidence suggests that technology is neither a miracle nor a menace, and the most **judicious** approach is to ask what problem a tool solves before adopting it. Good pedagogy must come first, and technology should serve clear learning goals rather than lead them. Schools that combine reliable access, trained teachers, thoughtful rules, and a focus on human relationships are most likely to capture the benefits while limiting the harm.

parts.title: The Urban Habitat: Ecology, Inequity, and the Future of City Living
parts.directions: Read the passage and choose the best answer (A, B, C, or D) for each question.
passage: More than half of the world's population now lives in urban areas, according to a United Nations survey of 2014. Yet a city is far more than concrete, because it is a **heterogeneous** habitat in which buildings, parks, rivers, and roads support very different forms of life. This passage examines how nature, heat, and inequality interact in the modern city.

Urban biodiversity is often surprising, because tropical and subtropical cities can keep high diversity when small patches of habitat are retained, and some suburban properties reportedly support well over a thousand species. In temperate cities, however, urbanisation often favours non-native species while reducing native ones, which lowers overall species richness. A study of 463 bird species reportedly found that urban birds were generally larger, had broader diets, and fed more on the ground or in the air. Researchers describe this pattern as an urban wildlife syndrome, which may reduce behavioural diversity across populations.

Development removes suitable habitat and splits what remains with roads, neighbourhoods, and other barriers, and this fragmentation can reduce genetic variation, population size, and species richness. Corridors that link green spaces can improve the resilience of ecosystems by allowing species to move between patches. More broadly, green infrastructure such as parks, green roofs, and rain gardens manages stormwater, filters air, and provides habitat, and a 2019 meta-analysis reportedly found that it generally improved biodiversity compared with conventional infrastructure.

Cities are often noticeably warmer than the countryside around them. [1] The effect arises mainly because dark roofs, asphalt, and concrete absorb and store heat, while the loss of vegetation removes the cooling that evaporation provides. **[2]** Luke Howard's measurements in the early nineteenth century reportedly showed central London about 2.1 degrees Celsius warmer than the countryside at night. **[3]** A 2024 analysis of 110 cities reportedly found that street trees typically cool daytime air by about one to two degrees Celsius. **[4]** Heat waves, which climate change is making more intense, make the effect more dangerous.

Heat is not shared equally, because low-income neighbourhoods tend to have fewer trees and more dark, paved surfaces. A study of 108 American cities reportedly found that formerly redlined neighbourhoods, which were once marked as risky for lending, are on average about 2.6 degrees Celsius hotter than other areas. Another study reportedly found that communities of colour were more likely to live in high-intensity heat areas in all but six of the 175 largest urbanised areas. Older adults face particular danger, because **they** are more vulnerable to heat illness when nights stay warm and air conditioning is limited.

Planners have several tools, and a 2018 simulation for London reportedly found that cool roofs lowered average outdoor temperatures by 1.2 degrees Celsius, compared with 0.3 degrees for added tree cover. Trees nevertheless offer shade, cleaner air, and habitat, so most strategies combine several measures. In shrinking cities such as Detroit, vacant lots could become greenways, although polluted soils must be cleaned first. Whatever the method, greening must be **equitable**, because parks and trees that arrive in poor neighbourhoods can sometimes raise rents and push out the residents whom the projects were meant to help.

The urban habitat is therefore both an ecosystem and a social landscape, and the way cities manage heat, nature, and fairness will shape the lives of billions of people. Green spaces cool streets, clean the air, absorb rainwater, and offer places to rest and meet. Whether future cities share these benefits widely, or reserve them for wealthier districts, remains one of the central questions of urban design.

parts.guide_md:
**1. Phân tích đề bài:**
- Phần thi gồm 6 câu hỏi trong khoảng 3 phút và được chia thành 2 chủ đề quen thuộc.
- **Topic A (Friends):** Câu hỏi 1–3 tập trung vào tình bạn, tính cách cá nhân và những phẩm chất của một người bạn tốt.
- **Topic B (Study):** Câu hỏi 4–6 tập trung vào việc học tập, môn học yêu thích và phương pháp học hiệu quả.
- Giám khảo đánh giá khả năng giao tiếp tự nhiên, độ trôi chảy, từ vựng, ngữ pháp và phát âm.
- Nên dành khoảng 25–35 giây cho mỗi câu hỏi và phát triển ý cân bằng giữa hai chủ đề.

**2. Cách xây dựng bố cục khi nói (Organization):**
- Sử dụng công thức ARE: Answer – Reason – Example.
- **Ví dụ Topic A:** I think I am a good friend because I am always willing to listen and help my friends when they have problems.
- **Ví dụ Topic B:** My favourite subject is English because it helps me communicate with people from different countries.
- Luôn tự hỏi Why hoặc How để mở rộng câu trả lời.
- Khi chuyển chủ đề có thể nói: Besides spending time with friends, I also spend a lot of time studying.

**3. Chiến lược đạt điểm cao (Fluency, Vocabulary & Grammar):**
- Duy trì tốc độ nói ổn định và tránh khoảng lặng kéo dài.
- Topic A chủ yếu sử dụng hiện tại đơn để mô tả tính cách và mối quan hệ.
- Topic B dùng hiện tại đơn để nói về thói quen học tập và sở thích học tập.
- Nếu quên từ, hãy diễn đạt bằng từ đơn giản hoặc mô tả ý tưởng.
- Từ vựng Topic A: trustworthy (đáng tin cậy), supportive (hay giúp đỡ), friendship (tình bạn), get along well (hòa hợp).
- Từ vựng Topic B: learning methods (phương pháp học), academic performance (kết quả học tập), concentration (sự tập trung), study habits (thói quen học tập).
Cụm từ quan trọng nên dùng:
- Be there for someone – Luôn ở bên hỗ trợ ai đó.
- Build strong friendships – Xây dựng tình bạn bền vững.
- Trust each other – Tin tưởng lẫn nhau.
- Improve academic performance – Cải thiện kết quả học tập.
- Manage study time effectively – Quản lý thời gian học hiệu quả.
- Stay focused on learning goals – Tập trung vào mục tiêu học tập.
Từ nối khi nói (Linking Words):
- First of all – Trước hết.
- In addition – Thêm vào đó.
- Moreover – Hơn nữa.
- For example – Ví dụ.
- As a result – Kết quả là.
Cách thể hiện quan điểm tự nhiên:
- Personally, I think loyalty is one of the most important qualities in a friendship.
- In my opinion, a good friend should be honest and supportive.
- From my perspective, friendship plays an important role in our lives.
- I believe studying regularly is more effective than studying at the last minute.
- What I enjoy most about learning is gaining new knowledge.
- I think good study habits can help students achieve better results.

**4. Các lỗi thường gặp:**
- Trả lời quá ngắn mà không giải thích lý do.
- Chỉ liệt kê phẩm chất của bạn bè mà không đưa ví dụ.
- Nói về học tập quá chung chung và thiếu trải nghiệm cá nhân.
- Dùng sai thì khi nói về thói quen hiện tại.

**5. Chiến lược xử lý khi bí ý hoặc quên từ:**
- Dùng câu đệm: That is an interesting question, let me think for a second.
- Mô tả tính cách hoặc hành động thay vì cố nhớ từ chính xác.

PHẦN 3 · NÓI (Speaking)
Social Interaction
PART 1
3 phút
Let’s talk about friends.
1.
Do you think you are a good friend? Why or why not?
2.
What qualities do you look for in a friend?
3.
How important are friends in your life?
Now, let’s talk about your studies.
4.
What are you studying at the moment?
5.
Which subject do you enjoy studying the most? Why?
6.
What do you usually do to study effectively?
GHI CHÚ TRẢ LỜI
GỢI Ý TRẢ LỜI
1. Phân tích đề bài:
• Phần thi gồm 6 câu hỏi trong khoảng 3 phút và được chia thành 2 chủ đề quen thuộc.
• Topic A (Friends): Câu hỏi 1–3 tập trung vào tình bạn, tính cách cá nhân và những phẩm chất của một người bạn tốt.
• Topic B (Study): Câu hỏi 4–6 tập trung vào việc học tập, môn học yêu thích và phương pháp học hiệu quả.
• Giám khảo đánh giá khả năng giao tiếp tự nhiên, độ trôi chảy, từ vựng, ngữ pháp và phát âm.
• Nên dành khoảng 25–35 giây cho mỗi câu hỏi và phát triển ý cân bằng giữa hai chủ đề.
2. Cách xây dựng bố cục khi nói (Organization):
• Sử dụng công thức ARE: Answer – Reason – Example.
• Ví dụ Topic A: I think I am a good friend because I am always willing to listen and help my friends when they have
problems.
• Ví dụ Topic B: My favourite subject is English because it helps me communicate with people from different countries.
• Luôn tự hỏi Why hoặc How để mở rộng câu trả lời.
• Khi chuyển chủ đề có thể nói: Besides spending time with friends, I also spend a lot of time studying.
3. Chiến lược đạt điểm cao (Fluency, Vocabulary & Grammar):
• Duy trì tốc độ nói ổn định và tránh khoảng lặng kéo dài.
• Topic A chủ yếu sử dụng hiện tại đơn để mô tả tính cách và mối quan hệ.
• Topic B dùng hiện tại đơn để nói về thói quen học tập và sở thích học tập.
• Nếu quên từ, hãy diễn đạt bằng từ đơn giản hoặc mô tả ý tưởng.
• Từ vựng Topic A: trustworthy (đáng tin cậy), supportive (hay giúp đỡ), friendship (tình bạn), get along well (hòa hợp).
• Từ vựng Topic B: learning methods (phương pháp học), academic performance (kết quả học tập), concentration (sự
tập trung), study habits (thói quen học tập).
Cụm từ quan trọng nên dùng:
• Be there for someone – Luôn ở bên hỗ trợ ai đó.
• Build strong friendships – Xây dựng tình bạn bền vững.
• Trust each other – Tin tưởng lẫn nhau.
• Improve academic performance – Cải thiện kết quả học tập.
• Manage study time effectively – Quản lý thời gian học hiệu quả.
• Stay focused on learning goals – Tập trung vào mục tiêu học tập.
Từ nối khi nói (Linking Words):
• First of all – Trước hết.
• In addition – Thêm vào đó.
• Moreover – Hơn nữa.
• For example – Ví dụ.
• As a result – Kết quả là.
Cách thể hiện quan điểm tự nhiên:
• Personally, I think loyalty is one of the most important qualities in a friendship.
• In my opinion, a good friend should be honest and supportive.
• From my perspective, friendship plays an important role in our lives.
• I believe studying regularly is more effective than studying at the last minute.
• What I enjoy most about learning is gaining new knowledge.
• I think good study habits can help students achieve better results.
4. Các lỗi thường gặp:
• Trả lời quá ngắn mà không giải thích lý do.
• Chỉ liệt kê phẩm chất của bạn bè mà không đưa ví dụ.
• Nói về học tập quá chung chung và thiếu trải nghiệm cá nhân.
• Dùng sai thì khi nói về thói quen hiện tại.
5. Chiến lược xử lý khi bí ý hoặc quên từ:
• Dùng câu đệm: That is an interesting question, let me think for a second.
• Mô tả tính cách hoặc hành động thay vì cố nhớ từ chính xác.
• Nếu bí ý về bạn bè, hãy kể về một người bạn thân.
• Nếu bí ý về học tập, hãy nói về môn học hoặc hoạt động học tập gần đây nhất.
6. Tư duy làm bài nói:
• Hãy coi đây là một cuộc trò chuyện đời thường.
• Thể hiện ý kiến cá nhân và trải nghiệm thực tế.
• Sự tự nhiên và rõ ràng quan trọng hơn việc sử dụng từ vựng quá khó.
Solution Discussion
PART 2
4 phút
You discover that money has disappeared from your bank account and you need to take action immediately.
You are considering the following options:
• Option 1: Contact the bank's customer service immediately
• Option 2: Go directly to the nearest bank branch
• Option 3: Report the problem to the police first
Choose the best option and explain your reasons.
GHI CHÚ CHUẨN BỊ (1 PHÚT)
GỢI Ý TRẢ LỜI
1. Phân tích đề bài:
• Tình huống liên quan đến việc tài khoản ngân hàng bị mất tiền và cần xử lý khẩn cấp.
• Bạn cần đánh giá cả ba lựa chọn trước khi quyết định phương án tốt nhất.
• Giám khảo đánh giá khả năng lập luận, so sánh và đưa ra quyết định hợp lý.
• Thời gian khoảng 4 phút, nên dành một ít thời gian để lập dàn ý.
2. Cách xây dựng bố cục khi nói (Organization):
• Sử dụng cấu trúc State opinion – Give reasons – Compare – Conclude.
• Option 1 giúp phản ứng nhanh và có thể khóa tài khoản ngay lập tức.
• Option 2 cho phép trao đổi trực tiếp với nhân viên ngân hàng.
• Option 3 có thể cần thiết nếu vụ việc liên quan đến hành vi phạm pháp nghiêm trọng.
• Liên hệ đến tính khẩn cấp và mức độ hiệu quả của từng lựa chọn.
• Sử dụng từ nối đối lập khi so sánh ưu và nhược điểm.
3. Chiến lược đạt điểm cao (Fluency, Vocabulary & Grammar):
• Liên kết các lựa chọn bằng tiêu chí tốc độ, độ an toàn và tính hiệu quả.
• Dùng hiện tại đơn để mô tả từng lựa chọn.
• Dùng điều kiện loại 1 để dự đoán kết quả của mỗi hành động.
• Nếu quên từ chuyên môn, hãy mô tả tình huống bằng ngôn ngữ đơn giản.
Cụm từ quan trọng nên dùng:
• Bank account security – Bảo mật tài khoản ngân hàng.
• Unauthorized transaction – Giao dịch trái phép.
• Customer service hotline – Đường dây chăm sóc khách hàng.
• Freeze the account – Khóa tài khoản.
• Financial loss – Tổn thất tài chính.
• Report suspicious activity – Báo cáo hoạt động đáng ngờ.
Từ nối khi nói (Linking Words):
• Firstly – Đầu tiên.
• However – Tuy nhiên.
• Compared with – So với.
• Furthermore – Hơn nữa.
• Therefore – Vì vậy.
Cách thể hiện quan điểm tự nhiên:
• I would choose contacting the bank immediately because time is extremely important in this situation.
• Compared with going to a branch, calling customer service may be faster.
• In my opinion, protecting the account should be the first priority.
4. Các lỗi thường gặp:
• Chỉ tập trung vào phương án được chọn mà không đánh giá các phương án khác.
• Lặp lại từ important hoặc good quá nhiều.
• Không đưa ra quyết định cuối cùng rõ ràng.
5. Chiến lược xử lý khi bí ý hoặc quên từ:
• Nếu quên từ chuyên môn, hãy nói về việc bảo vệ tiền hoặc tài khoản.
• Dùng câu đệm: Let's evaluate this option from a different perspective.
• Nếu bí ý, hãy so sánh tốc độ xử lý và tính an toàn của từng lựa chọn.
6. Tư duy làm bài nói:
• Hãy suy nghĩ như người đang gặp tình huống thực tế.
• Ưu tiên giải pháp nhanh chóng, hiệu quả và an toàn nhất.
